passage:
Before the maths exam in the school hall, Aman took out his lucky blue pencil, the one with bite marks, and tapped the desk three times. Then three more, just in case.
Gopika, at the next desk, whispered, "You know a pencil can't do sums, right?"
"I know," Aman whispered back. "But last time I forgot it and got a C."
"Last time you didn't revise."
Aman went red. "Still. I feel better with it."
Sangeeta Ma'am, walking the rows, noticed the tapping. She didn't take the pencil. She stopped by his desk and said quietly, "Lucky pencil's fine. Your revision is what does the work." Aman nodded and started on question one.

qa.q: How did Aman tap the desk before the exam?
qa.a: Three times, then three more, just in case.

qa.q: Why does Aman keep the pencil even though he knows it can't do sums?
qa.a: It makes him feel safer and calmer, and he links forgetting it with the C, even though skipping revision was the real cause.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta Ma'am do that helped?
qa.a: She let him keep the harmless pencil but reminded him that revision does the work, so the ritual doesn't replace effort.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Aman's ritual?
qa.a: Gopika finds it a bit silly, and points out that the missing revision, not the pencil, explains the C.

grounding: A boy taps his desk and carries a lucky pencil into an exam, half knowing it is illogical but feeling safer with it.

passage:
My brother Sahil is ten, and he walks to school like the pavement is lava. He hops over every crack. If he steps on one by mistake, he goes back and steps on it with the other foot, "to even it out."
On match days he wears the same green T-shirt, the one with the hole at the collar. Mummy has tried to wash it twice; he gets upset.
I'm Dolma, I'm thirteen, and I once asked him if he really thinks cracks matter. He shrugged. "Probably not. But what if?"
I can't see inside his head. He does seem calmer after hopping, and he still practises batting every evening. So I've stopped teasing him.

qa.q: What does Sahil wear on match days?
qa.a: The same green T-shirt, the one with the hole at the collar.

qa.q: What does Sahil's 'Probably not. But what if?' show about his thinking?
qa.a: He half knows cracks don't matter, but the ritual still feels safer, just in case.

qa.q: When is Sahil's habit harmless, and what would make it worth talking about?
qa.a: It's harmless while he still practises batting every evening; it would be worth a gentle talk if it made him skip practice or became very upsetting.

qa.q: How might Mummy feel about the unwashed T-shirt?
qa.a: A bit frustrated about washing it, but she has seen how much it matters to him.

grounding: An older sibling describes a ten-year-old brother avoiding cracks and wearing a lucky shirt while half admitting it is not logical.

passage:
Sunday. Samir laid out his lucky shirt, the checked one he wore when he won the spelling bee. "Tomorrow's science test needs it," he told Francis on the phone.
Monday. After the night's rain, the shirt was still wet on the line. Samir's stomach dropped. He wore a plain one and kept touching his collar all morning, sure he'd mess up. Francis passed him a note: "It's just a shirt. You know the stuff."
Thursday. Results came back: eighteen out of twenty. Samir stared at the paper. "Maybe it was never the shirt," he told Francis. Then, after a pause: "I'm still wearing it for the final, though."

qa.q: What score did Samir get in the science test?
qa.a: Eighteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why did Samir's stomach drop when he saw the wet shirt?
qa.a: The shirt made him feel safe, so without it he felt unprotected and sure he would mess up.

qa.q: What could Samir tell himself the next time the ritual isn't possible?
qa.a: That he scored eighteen out of twenty without it, so his own revision is what counts.

qa.q: How does Francis help Samir through Monday?
qa.a: Francis passes a note saying it's just a shirt and he knows the stuff, which is caring and down to earth.

grounding: Across a week, a boy relies on a lucky shirt, does well without it, and half admits it is not the cause while still wanting it.

passage: Raghav, before your exam, let your Hemant Dadu tell you something. When I was eleven, in our town in Satara, I had a rule. Before every test I touched the school gate three times with my left hand, then walked in without stepping on the shadow of the flagpole. Every single time. My friends laughed. I laughed too, a bit, because I knew a gate can't give marks. But the one morning I forgot, I sat in the maths test sweating, sure I'd fail. I didn't fail, by the way. I got my usual marks. Still, next time, three taps. For years. Even now, before the doctor's appointments, I sometimes tap the doorframe. So if you have your lucky pencil, keep it, beta. Just make sure you've also opened the book.

qa.q: How many times did Dadu touch the school gate before each test?
qa.a: Three times, with his left hand.

qa.q: Why did Dadu keep tapping the gate even though he knew it couldn't give marks?
qa.a: It made him feel safer and calmer before tests, and the one time he forgot, he felt anxious, so the ritual stayed.

qa.q: What balance does Dadu suggest for Raghav's lucky pencil?
qa.a: He suggests keeping the pencil for comfort but making sure he also studies, so the ritual never replaces the work.

qa.q: How might Dadu's friends have seen his gate-tapping back then?
qa.a: They laughed at it, finding it funny, though they may not have known how nervous he felt without it.

grounding: An elder recalls his childhood lucky ritual before tests, which he half knew was illogical but still felt safer doing.

passage: Exam day in Kochi, and the rain had flooded the lane. The school bus was late, and Jomon, ten, couldn't find his lucky eraser, the green one shaped like a fish. He turned his bag upside down on the floor. "Amma, it's gone. I'll fail." Seema, his mother, was holding his umbrella and the bus was honking. "Jomon, it's an eraser." "I know it's silly!" he said, voice cracking. "But I feel safer with it." Seema glanced at the clock, then at his face. She opened her own bag and pulled out a small green paper clip. "Here, borrow this one. It's green too." He looked at it, half-laughing, and put it in his pencil box. On the way, stepping over puddles, he still avoided every crack in the pavement. At school he wrote the whole paper.

qa.q: What shape was Jomon's lucky eraser?
qa.a: It was green and shaped like a fish.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he said, "I know it's silly!"
qa.a: He felt torn: embarrassed because he half knew an eraser couldn't help, yet anxious because he still felt safer with it.

qa.q: What did Seema choose to do under time pressure, and why did it help?
qa.a: She gave him a green paper clip as a stand-in, calming him quickly without mocking him, so he could get to school and write the exam.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Seema, with rain, a late bus and a missing eraser?
qa.a: It was rushed and stressful for her, but she still paused to look at Jomon's face and respond kindly.

grounding: On a rainy exam morning, a boy panics without his lucky eraser and avoids cracks, half knowing it is not logical.
